sections.title: Transitive and Intransitive
sections.content:
Some verbs can be either transitive or intransitive, allowing us to focus on either the person or thing performing the action, or the person or thing affected by the action. Compare:
• She closed the door. (transitive) and The door closed. (intransitive)
• I've ripped my shirt. (transitive) and My shirt has ripped. (intransitive)
Also: begin, bend, break, burn, change, decrease, drop, finish, increase, move, open, shut, start, vary, wake (most are 'change' verbs)

sections.title: Transitive verbs without objects
sections.content:
Some transitive verbs don't need an object when the meaning is clear from the context:
• I often sing (songs) in the shower.
• She plays (the saxophone) beautifully.
Also: answer, ask, change, cook, dance, drink, drive, eat, fail, park, phone, read, smoke, study, wash, wash up, wave, win, write

sections.title: Complements
sections.content:
After some verbs we usually add a complement – a phrase which completes the meaning of a verb, noun or adjective – which is an adverb or prepositional phrase:
• The disease originated in Britain. (not The disease originated.)
Other verbs usually have a complement but may not. Compare:
• He paused for a few moments. and He paused. (no complement needed)

sections.title: Verbs + Preposition + Object
sections.content:
Some verbs are commonly followed by a particular preposition or prepositions and then an object:
• We had to deal with hundreds of complaints. (not We had to deal.)
• I'm sure that blue car belongs to Murad. (not I'm sure that blue car belongs.)
Also: adhere to, aspire to, culminate in / with, detract from, differentiate between, incline to / towards, specialise in

sections.title: Object + prepositional phrase complement
sections.content:
Some verbs are usually followed by an object + prepositional phrase complement:
• I always associate pizza with Italy. (not I always associate pizza.)
• She put the report on the floor. (not She put the report.)
Also: attribute ... to, base ... on / upon, equate ... with, inflict ... on, mistake ... for, regard ... as / with, remind ... of

sections.title: Object + adjective complement
sections.content:
Some verbs are often followed by an object + adjective (or adjective phrase) complement:
• The people of this country will hold the government responsible.
• Conti pronounced herself fit for the match.
Also: assume, believe, consider, declare, find, judge, prove, report, think.

exercises.question: Aya was (reading) a book when the telephone rang. (Is 'a book' omittable?)
exercises.hint: Read is a verb where the object can be omitted if clear from context.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: (a book)
Read is a verb where the object can be omitted if clear from context. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: Would you like to come over to eat dinner tonight? (Is 'dinner' omittable?)
exercises.hint: Eat is a verb where the object can be omitted.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: eat (dinner)
Eat is a verb where the object can be omitted.

exercises.sentence: I find very difficult to concentrate when there is background noise.
exercises.correction: I find it very difficult to concentrate when there is background noise.
acceptable: I find it very difficult to concentrate
exercises.hint: 'Find + adjective + to-infinitive' needs 'it' as a placeholder object.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I find it very difficult to concentrate
When 'find' (or 'make', 'consider', 'think') is followed by an adjective + to-infinitive, a dummy 'it' is required as the grammatical object: 'find it difficult to...', 'make it clear that...', 'consider it essential to...'. Without 'it', the sentence is grammatically incomplete.

exercises.question: She washed herself... (Is 'herself' omittable?)
exercises.hint: Wash can be used intransitively when referring to oneself.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: washed (herself)
Wash can be used intransitively when referring to oneself.

exercises.question: ...reached their house... (Is 'their house' omittable?)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: reached their house
Reach usually requires an object. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.sentence: She explained me the reasons for her decision in detail.
exercises.correction: She explained the reasons for her decision to me in detail.
exercises.hint: 'Explain' cannot take a double object — use 'explain X to Y'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She explained the reasons to me
'Explain' does not follow the double-object pattern. Unlike 'give', 'send', 'show', 'tell', you cannot say 'explain someone something'. The pattern is: explain + thing explained + to + person. The same applies to 'describe', 'suggest', 'propose', 'recommend'.

exercises.question: Electors deserve more from a political party that ___ national leadership.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: aspires to
The verb 'aspire' is followed by 'to' + noun phrase (aspire to greatness) or 'to + infinitive' (aspire to become). It is not followed directly by a bare noun without 'to'.

exercises.question: Years of research by Fleming ___ the discovery of penicillin.
exercises.hint: Culminate can take in or with.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both are possible
'Culminate' can be followed by either 'in' or 'with': 'culminate in a disaster' or 'culminate with a speech'. Both prepositions are standard; 'in' is slightly more common.

exercises.question: The committee considered ___ necessary to review the entire policy from scratch.
exercises.hint: Dummy 'it' needed before the adjective complement.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: it
After 'consider/find/make/think + adjective + to-infinitive', insert 'it' as a placeholder object. The to-infinitive ('to review the entire policy') is the real subject, but English requires 'it' in this position to maintain SVO word order.

exercises.question: It was dark and raining and she ___ the black car ___ a taxi.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: mistook / for
The pattern is: 'mistake X for Y' — you think X is actually Y. The preposition 'for' is fixed in this idiom. Do not confuse with 'confuse X with Y'.

exercises.question: The scientific evidence proved him ___.
options: Both guilty and to be guilty
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both guilty and to be guilty
Both are possible formal structures.

exercises.question: She declared herself ___ with the result.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: familiar
After 'declare', the pattern is: declare + object + adjective or noun (declare yourself satisfied / declare the meeting closed). This is an object complement structure.

exercises.question: They considered the food ___.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: smelly
After 'consider', the pattern is: consider + object + adjective or noun (consider the matter closed / consider her brilliant). This is an object complement. 'Consider' does not take 'to be' in current usage.
